title: pipeline-stage-latency-mosaic
content:
Summary:
This note captures a stage-by-stage end-to-end latency profile ('mosaic') across representative workloads and model variants. The goal: identify the highest contributors to p99 tail and practical mitigations that preserve p50 while reducing p95/p99 for production traffic.

Context and motivation:
- Recent customer reports (INF-842) show spikes in p99 latency for small-chat workloads (<=128 tokens) during peak hours. p50 is stable but tail is variable.
- We suspect interplay between routing/queue jitter and model-side KV cache misses (cold KV merges) amplified by batching edge cases.
- Instead of a single trace decomposition, this mosaic aggregates stage distributions across slices (model variant, batch size, prompt length) to highlight recurring bottlenecks.

Slicing strategy (why these slices):
- Small prompt / batch=1 (chat real-time): fast-path, sensitive to fixed stage overheads.
- Small prompt / batch=8 (burst): exposes batch-join and queue latency effects.
- Long prompt / batch=1 (context-heavy): dominates token-gen time and KV overheads.
- Model variants: alpha-1 (FP16), alpha-2-int8 (INT8 quantized), fallback-small (compact small model).
- Traffic class: hosted-api tier vs dedicated-reserved (different routing).

Stages (canonical names used in traces):
- ingress-auth (auth + quota)
- parse-req (http parse + proto)
- route-decision (policy + model selection)
- prequeue (local checks + trace attach)
- queue-wait (time spent waiting for batch formation)
- batch-join (synchronization on batch boundary)
- kv-fetch (distributed KV read for prefix cache)
- model-init (model sharded init or cold worker spin-up)
- forward (actual model forward / kernel execution)
- kv-merge (merge KV during generation)
- token-emit (postprocess + detokenize + response streaming)
- egress (network send + flush)

Representative numbers (aggregated p50/p95/p99 in ms) - Small prompt <=128 tokens, batch=1, model alpha-1 (FP16):
- ingress-auth: p50 1.2, p95 2.1, p99 5.0
- parse-req: p50 0.9, p95 1.8, p99 4.2
- route-decision: p50 0.8, p95 2.4, p99 6.6  <-- variability due to policy DB timeouts
- prequeue: p50 0.6, p95 1.1, p99 3.0
- queue-wait: p50 0.5, p95 6.3, p99 28.0  <-- high tail during microbursts
- batch-join: p50 0.7, p95 3.8, p99 19.2
- kv-fetch: p50 2.2, p95 8.6, p99 46.0  <-- dominant tail contributor for p99
- model-init: p50 0.5, p95 1.9, p99 12.4
- forward: p50 14.0, p95 18.6, p99 30.1
- kv-merge: p50 0.6, p95 2.5, p99 10.8
- token-emit: p50 1.6, p95 3.2, p99 8.9
- egress: p50 0.4, p95 1.0, p99 2.5
Total E2E: p50 ~24.0ms, p95 ~52.3ms, p99 ~171.7ms (observed distribution)

Notes on this slice: p99 dominated by kv-fetch and queue/batch jitter. Forward contributes but less extreme.

Representative numbers - Small prompt, batch=8, model alpha-1 (FP16):
- queue-wait: p50 4.2, p95 18.3, p99 72.8
- batch-join: p50 8.1, p95 26.7, p99 110.4
- forward: p50 14.0, p95 18.9, p99 31.2
- kv-fetch: p50 2.2, p95 9.0, p99 50.3
Total E2E p99 often exceeds 250ms in congested hosts (burst windows).

Representative numbers - Long prompt >=1024 tokens, batch=1, model alpha-2-int8 (INT8):
- forward dominates: p50 120ms, p95 230ms, p99 410ms
- kv-fetch p99 still large for long prefixes: p99 88ms
- token-emit p99 40ms (detokenize + streaming burst)
Total E2E p99 ~640ms for worst-case long prompts (observed in dedicated tests).

What the mosaic shows (high-level findings):
1) Two distinct tail modes: short-prompt microburst mode (queue/batch / sync jitter) and long-prompt compute-heavy mode (forward + kv).
2) kv-fetch is disproportionately present in p99 across slices. Even small prompts see kv-tail due to occasional cache miss patterns and cross-host KV reads.
3) Batch-join/synchronization amplifies tail when traffic is bursty; this is visible at p95->p99 gap scaling with batch size.
4) route-decision variability correlates with external policy DB latency spikes (timeouts cause tens of ms jumps).

Data collection methodology and queries used:
- Trace collection: ri-trace-collect --service serving-runtime --sample-rate 1/1000 --tags slice=prod-mosaic --out traces/2024-04-mosaic.ndjson
- Host metrics: vmstat/iostat and GPU metrics collected with perf-agent v2.1 (nvml sampling @100ms) aligned with trace ids.
- Aggregation script (psuedocode SQL used for heatmap):
  SELECT slice, stage, percentile(duration_ms, 50) as p50, percentile(duration_ms,95) as p95, percentile(duration_ms,99) as p99, count(*)
  FROM trace_spans
  WHERE trace_time BETWEEN '2024-04-20' AND '2024-04-27' AND model IN ('alpha-1','alpha-2-int8') AND batch_size IN (1,8)
  GROUP BY slice, stage
  ORDER BY slice, stage

Sampling caveats and biases:
- Sample rate 1/1000 biases against extremely rare microstates; we augmented with targeted 1/50 sampling for peak windows.
- Some traces have incomplete spans when worker crashed; we filter by traces with full span coverage.
- Dedicated instances show lower route-decision variance but similar kv tail (indicates KV layer independent of host type).

Root-cause hypotheses and evidence links:
1) KV cold reads across host boundary: correlated with cross-rack network latency and backend KV node GC cycles. Evidence: trace://2024-04-27/0a1b2c3d and NVMe I/O spikes at 2024-04-26T16:03Z.
2) Batch synchronization jitter: caused by uneven request arrival times from edge routers during traffic bursts; evidence: synchronized batch-join peaks in traces and edge router metrics (PR: serving-runtime#4123).
3) Route-decision slow-paths: configuration lookup hitting third-party policy service; adding local cache reduces p95/p99 for route stage.

Quick mitigation experiments attempted (results):
- Prewarm KV cache on worker startup: reduced kv-fetch p99 from ~46ms -> ~12ms for cold-start traces in canary (20% traffic).
- Adaptive batching window: dynamic max-wait (ms) reduced batch-join p99 from 110ms -> 64ms at cost of 3% throughput loss.
- Local policy cache (TTL 30s): route-decision p99 reduced by 55% in canary.

Actionable next steps (short-term):
- Rollout KV prewarm for hosted-api workers (config flag) to canary 10% this week (owner: Priya).
- Implement soft-degrade for batch-join: if queue-wait > X ms, flip to immediate-forward path to avoid tail amplification (owner: Jordan).
- Add route-decision local caching with stats and fallback (owner: Aisha).
- Run a focused 24h trace capture at 1/50 during next traffic spike window (owner: Marcus).

Longer-term proposals (2-3 sprints):
- Rework KV layer for async prefetching of likely prefixes (heuristic based on recent prompts).
- Explore per-worker microsharding of KV to reduce cross-host reads.
- Investigate kernel-level forward optimizations for alpha-2-int8 to compress p99 forward times.

Appendix: example commands and helpers used during investigation:
- Collect traces for a given host: ri-trace-collect --host host-42 --out host-42-traces.ndjson --start 2024-04-26T15:00 --end 2024-04-26T17:00
- Align nvml/GPU traces: perf-agent fetch --host host-42 --metric nvml --start ... --out nvml-host-42.csv
- Quick aggregator (python): python -m scripts/trace_agg --input traces/*.ndjson --group-by stage --percentiles 50 95 99 --out mosaic-agg.csv

Open questions / TODOs:
- What causes sporadic KV node GC pauses? Need infra to check KV cluster GC logs and compactions.
- How many real customers see noticeable degradation vs synthetic benchmarks? Coordinate with CS to pull customer-facing error reports.
- Evaluate cost/benefit of adaptive batching vs throughput SLA. Run throughput regression tests after changes.

Trace examples to inspect interactively:
- trace://2024-04-27/0a1b2c3d — kv tail, includes NVMe I/O spike
- trace://2024-04-29/7f9e8d6c — batch-join tail during burst window (edge router correlated)

Conclusions:
- Reducing p99 requires multiple coordinated mitigations: KV prewarm + local policy cache + adaptive batching. Each reduces a distinct tail mode.
- Short-term fixes (KV prewarm, route cache) are low-risk and high-impact; prioritize for canary rollout.
- Continue to use mosaic aggregation across slices rather than single-trace narratives — it surfaces consistent cross-slice bottlenecks.

Notes to reviewers:
- Please validate findings against your own trace slices (especially dedicated vs hosted).
- Feedback sought on thresholds for adaptive batching and acceptable throughput loss.
- If you add experimental results, include full trace ids and sampling parameters for reproducibility.

-- Marcus
